account: A woman with locked-in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) received the Utrecht NeuroProsthesis in October 2015. After training, she selected letters and called a caregiver by attempting to move her hand. The makers reported that 28 weeks after electrode placement she controlled a computer typing program accurately and independently, at the equivalent of two letters per minute. Seven to nine months after surgery, she rated the implant and her own eye tracker on the Psychosocial Impact of Assistive Devices Scale. She scored the implant 1.1 for competence, 2.2 for adaptability and 1.0 for self-esteem, and the eye tracker 1.3, 1.5 and 0.6. Writing in Scientific American on 17 November 2016, R. Douglas Fields reported that Andrew Schwartz of the University of Pittsburgh, who was not involved in the study, called the result a significant achievement. Niels Birbaumer of Tübingen University warned that such implants may carry an unknown risk for people with advanced ALS, and Phillip Kennedy of Neural Signals said that one to two letters a minute did not justify a craniotomy. Caregivers set up the equipment, but she then used it without research staff. It became her only technological means of communication after she lost reliable eye tracking. Home use continued for nearly seven years. Nighttime use stopped in October 2022, and home use ended in March 2023 as control became unreliable. Researchers considered ALS-related brain changes the likely explanation, without proving a single cause. The documented decoder combined brain-signal features and fitted thresholds. The sources name no machine-learning model.

ai_role.statement: The documented decoder combines normalized brain-signal features and fitted thresholds to generate clicks. Whether that mechanism qualifies as AI remains unresolved. The communication benefit itself is documented.
